The mechanism: `createClient()` calls `impersonated.auth.setSession({ access_token, refresh_token })` with the SAME two tokens read back from the one-time-written `tt_impersonation` cookie on every request; Supabase rotates refresh tokens on use by default, so the FIRST request after the access token's own natural expiry refreshes successfully in-memory (never persisted back to the cookie - nothing in this codebase does that), and every request AFTER that presents an already-rotated, now-invalid refresh token.

**4. Built a real, independent, live reproduction of that exact failure - not a re-read of `GoTrueClient.js`, which is as far as the prior pass's own analysis went.** A disposable Node script (`impersonation_refresh_repro.js`, written to and deleted from this session's own scratchpad, never the repo) spun up a real local HTTP server standing in for Supabase's Auth API (`POST /auth/v1/token?grant_type=refresh_token` returning the real documented 400 `invalid_grant`/`"Invalid Refresh Token: Already Used"` shape) and a real local REST stand-in, then exercised the REAL, unmodified `@supabase/supabase-js` package (the exact one `lib/supabase/server.ts` imports, resolved from `app/node_modules` via `NODE_PATH`) against it - a genuine live repro, not a mock of the SDK itself. Fed it an expired-but-structurally-valid access token (`decodeJWT` doesn't verify the signature client-side, so a `header.payload.sig` triple with a past `exp` decodes fine) plus the rotated refresh token, exactly matching the real cookie's post-rotation state:
   - `setSession()` made exactly one real network call to the mock refresh endpoint, confirming the refresh really is attempted (not skipped) - then **returned gracefully, did not throw**: `{ data: { session: null }, error: { name: "AuthApiError", message: "Invalid Refresh Token: Already Used", status: 400 } }`. `createClient()` itself never checks this return value at all (just `await`s it and returns `impersonated` regardless) - fine, precisely because nothing here throws.
   - The SAME broken client's subsequent `.auth.getUser()` (the exact call nearly every Server Component/Action in this app makes next) also did not throw: `{ user: null, error: AuthSessionMissingError }` - every one of this app's existing `if (!user) redirect(...)`-shaped guards handles this correctly already (it's the same shape as "not signed in at all").
   - The SAME client's `.from("tenders").select("id").limit(1)` (the realistic next call a page would actually make) reached the mock REST backend with `Authorization: Bearer <the ANON key>` and `apikey: <the ANON key>` - **anonymous privilege, not the admin's own elevated session and not the impersonated target's**, confirming the earlier write-up's "falls back to an unauthenticated/anonymous Supabase client" claim as the literal, demonstrated mechanism rather than an inference.
   - Separately tried a non-JWT-shaped (fully garbage) access token string too, in case a differently-tampered cookie value hits a different code path: also no throw, `AuthInvalidJwtError`, zero network calls even attempted (the JWT-structure check runs before any request) - the fail-safe behavior holds even for a malformed/tampered cookie, not just an expired-but-well-formed one.

**5. Conclusion - the standing record is corrected/strengthened, not changed in substance.** This is still a real, unfixed robustness gap (an admin's impersonation session can silently stop working well inside its documented 4-hour window, with no clear error message - a genuine UX/diagnostics problem, matching the existing write-up's own framing) but it is now **live-repro-confirmed**, not merely reasoned about, to fail safe: no exception propagates to crash a request, no privilege escalation results, and the fallback is provably anonymous-RLS-role, never the admin's own real session or the target's. This directly answers the task brief's own question ("worth a fresh, careful look at whether it's exploitable") with a demonstrated no: not exploitable as a security issue, on every path this repro could reach without live Supabase credentials (which remain unavailable in this sandbox, same limitation the original write-up already stated). **Not fixed this pass** - same reasoning as before (the correct fix needs middleware-level cookie-refresh handling across every request shape, real surface area in a security-sensitive path, and no live Supabase project to verify an end-to-end fix actually works) - this pass's contribution is tightening the verification of the failure mode itself, not building the fix.

Severity stated honestly, not inflated to Finding 267's own bar: no token/secret in the resulting link, the email only ever goes to the same user whose own request triggered it, and whether an attacker can actually get an unregistered `Host` value past Vercel's own production edge routing was not independently confirmed from this sandbox (no outbound probe of the live `tenderready.app` routing was possible) - what IS conclusively confirmed is that the function's own code applies no validation at all and contradicts its own stated contract, and is the one exception to how every OTHER email-link builder in this exact repo already does this (`scripts/send-deadline-reminders.ts`/`send-discovered-tenders.ts`/`send-operational-alerts.ts` all read `process.env.APP_URL`; `lib/emailBrand.ts`'s own default and `scripts/render-email-samples.ts`/`lib/emailTemplateSamples.ts`'s own `APP_URL` constants are all the literal real production domain, `tenderready.app`, confirmed via `grep -rn "tenderready.app" app` - 10 real hits, all either the literal domain or an explicit env-var read). It could: `isSafeRedirectPath()`'s `/^\/(?!\/|\\)/` only inspects the character immediately after the leading `/`, but every real browser's URL parser strips ASCII tab/LF/CR from the ENTIRE string, anywhere, before resolving it - so `"/\t/evil.com"`/`"/\t\\evil.com"` pass the regex (the next character is a tab, neither `/` nor `\`) while the value a browser actually navigates to, once that tab is gone, re-forms the exact bypass shape this file exists to block. Confirmed this is a REAL navigation bypass with a real browser, not a parser-level curiosity: started the real dev server, drove a small temporary scratch route (removed before finishing, never committed) calling the exact same `useRouter().push()` mechanism `login/page.tsx`'s own post-sign-in redirect uses, with Playwright/Chromium - pre-fix, `router.push("/\t\\evil.example.com")` issued a real outbound HTTP request to `http://evil.example.com/` (`net::ERR_NAME_NOT_RESOLVED` only because the sandbox has no DNS for that host, confirmed via the captured `request`/`requestfailed` events and `page.url()` landing on `chrome-error://chromewebdata/`, i.e. a failed CROSS-ORIGIN load attempt, not a same-origin page). Traced the mechanism in Next.js's own router source (`app-router.js`): it resolves the pushed URL, detects the cross-origin result, and falls back to a real `location.assign()` call - an API with no same-origin restriction, unlike `history.pushState()`. Fixed by stripping tab/CR/LF the same way a browser's own parser does, before the existing check - confirmed this doesn't narrow legitimate paths (a control case with a tab elsewhere in an otherwise-safe path, which doesn't reform the bypass shape after stripping, still correctly passes). Verified red-then-green against the real function (`npx vitest run lib/safeRedirect.spec.ts`: 1 failed/9 passed pre-fix, 10/10 post-fix) AND re-ran the identical live-browser repro against the fixed code: zero requests to `evil.example.com`, landed on the app's own real `/login` redirect instead. ## This pass (2026-11-09lxxiii, standing solution-architect review, background worker): took up the task brief's own option (a) - independently re-verified the `lxxii` pass's own `create_company_invite_checked()` "related-but-not-independently-exploitable" observation, rather than just trusting its write-up. **The "not exploitable" conclusion was itself wrong, in a real and fixable way.** `redeem_company_invite()`'s own LATER write (`update people ... where id = ... and company_id = ...`) is correctly company-scoped, as `lxxii` claimed - but the SAME function's EARLIER gating read (the `select linked_user_id ... for update` that feeds its "already linked to a different account" exception, added by `0122`) has NO such filter. Combined with `create_company_invite_checked()`'s own missing validation (the part `lxxii` already flagged), this is a real cross-tenant information-disclosure oracle: any company admin can name a complete stranger's real `people.id` from a different company on an invite into their OWN company, redeem it with a second mailbox they control, and learn - from whether it raises or not - whether that stranger's person row already has a linked user account. Reproduced live, RED, against the real unmodified `0113`/`0122` code in a disposable scratch Postgres: two invites targeting two different Company-B people (one already linked, one not) produced two cleanly divergent, state-revealing outcomes for an attacker with zero relationship to Company B. Checked the two live crons that actually send those reminders (`deadline-reminders.yml` 04:10 UTC, `compliance-alerts.yml` 03:30 UTC) - both outside the 22:00-24:00 UTC bad window, so today's scheduled sends happen not to be desynced by this particular coincidence of timing, but every live page render during the 2-hour SAST window was genuinely wrong until this fix, and the reminder scripts would silently mis-fire the moment either cron's time is ever moved without anyone connecting it to this.

Reproduced live, real command, real crash - not reasoned about.** Built a real `profile.json` (same shape `process_cv_jobs.py`'s own `self_test()` uses) with `key_people[0].name` set to a 5000-character string - plausible, not contrived: `people.name` is a plain `text not null` column with no length constraint, no form-side `maxLength`, and is also a field `extract_cv_fields.py`'s AI extraction can propose from a misread CV. Ran `python3 generate_cv.py profile.json 0 <out_dir> --format sanral_keyperson --detail summary`, the real CLI entry point `process_cv_jobs.py`/`harness_pack.py` both call into. **Crashed**: `OSError: [Errno 36] File name too long`, traced to `doc.save(docx_path)` - `_safe_name()` strips forbidden characters but never truncates, so the full 5000 characters land in the final filename, well past the ~255-byte limit most Linux filesystems enforce.

**Root cause: a stated convention that was never actually followed.** `_safe_name()`'s own docstring claims parity with "the app's own upload actions" - true for the character-stripping regex, but the real TS-side function it's modelled on, `app/lib/safeFileName.ts`, also truncates (`.slice(0, 120)`); the Python side never did. Checked both real callers rather than assuming: `process_cv_jobs.py`'s `process_job()` wraps the whole job in a broad `except Exception`, so in the main production worker this crash is caught, correctly marks the job `failed` with a clear customer message, and raises a system alert - not silent, but still an avoidable real failure. `engine/pack/harness_pack.py`'s own call site wraps `generate_cv.generate()` in `except ValueError` ONLY (line 157) - an `OSError` is not a `ValueError`, so there this exact crash is NOT caught and aborts the whole harness pack build for every other position too, not just the long-named one.

**Fix:** `_safe_name()` now truncates its sanitized result to 80 characters. Picked shorter than the TS file's 120 deliberately - this function returns only the name *portion* of the final filename, and every real caller appends its own `_{format}_{detail}_{mode}[_{job_id}]` suffix plus an extension on top, so 80 leaves comfortable headroom while keeping the full filename well under the 255-byte limit regardless of caller.

Inspected the real output, not just the exit code: the written `.docx` (119-character filename, confirmed under the limit) opens cleanly via `python-docx` (13 real paragraphs, correct heading text); the matching LibreOffice-converted `.pdf` opens via `pypdf` (5 real pages) - a genuinely usable document.

**3. Read `app/app/api/billing/payfast/itn/route.ts` and `apply_payfast_itn()` (0112, the latest body on `main`) in full first**, plus `app/app/api/billing/checkout/route.ts` and `lib/payfast.ts`'s `nextPeriodEnd()`. Established the one fact that makes this bug non-obvious: `checkout/route.ts` sets `subscription_type: "1"`, `cycles: 0` - a genuine PayFast RECURRING subscription - so `m_payment_id` is minted ONCE at initial checkout and reused for EVERY future renewal charge under that subscription's whole lifetime, BY DESIGN. A naive "have we already activated this `m_payment_id`?" idempotency check would have been wrong - it would break real monthly/yearly renewals, which legitimately call `apply_payfast_itn()` again and again for the same `m_payment_id`, each time correctly extending `current_period_end`. The field that genuinely IS unique per real transaction - PayFast's own `pf_payment_id` (the route's `p_payfast_token`) - was never read back against the row's own stored value anywhere in the function; only ever written into it.

**Confirmed live, real scratch Postgres, not reasoned about.** `service postgresql start`; replayed all 114 migrations clean (`engine/security/replay_schema.sh`). Seeded a company with a trialing subscription (the real `start_company_trial()` trigger's own row) set to `starter`/`monthly` with a real `payfast_m_payment_id`. First `COMPLETE` ITN (`pf_payment_id='pf-token-1'`, amount `1490`, the real starter/monthly price) correctly activated it: `current_period_end` = now + 31 days. **Redelivering the IDENTICAL ITN** - same `m_payment_id` AND same `pf_payment_id`, same amount, "arriving" 10 days later (`p_period_end` is always recomputed by the route as `nextPeriodEnd()` at CALL time, never carried over from the original delivery) - against the pre-fix function: `current_period_end` jumped from `2026-12-10` to `2026-12-20` and `current_period_start` reset to the redelivery's own "now" - **a free 10-day extension of a paid subscription, zero new payment, compounding with every redelivery.** A genuinely NEW renewal charge for the same subscription (same `m_payment_id`, a DIFFERENT `pf_payment_id`, exactly as PayFast issues per real charge) was separately confirmed to still correctly extend the period - the bug is specifically the SAME-`pf_payment_id` case, not recurring billing in general.

**Why this is realistic, not contrived:** PayFast's own merchant dashboard has a documented manual "Resend ITN" action, legitimately used well after a charge already settled; separately, PayFast's documented retry behaviour fires again whenever IT didn't receive our 200 even though we actually processed it (a dropped response, a proxy timeout) - a transient network blip is enough, not an attack. There is no replay-prevention nonce/timestamp on a PayFast ITN at all - the three existing checks (signature, source IP, server confirmation) all legitimately re-pass on an exact replay of a real past ITN.

**Fix, `app/supabase/migrations/0125_payfast_itn_exact_redelivery_idempotency.sql`:** before either `'active'`-path branch does anything else, if `p_payfast_token` is non-null, equals the row's own currently-stored `payfast_token`, AND the row's current `status` already equals what this ITN would set it to - it's a repeat of an already-fully-applied event, not a new charge - return as a no-op. A brand-new charge or first-ever activation is unaffected. **Re-verified green** against a freshly-replayed 115-migration database (not the hand-patched scratch one) with a new test file, `engine/security/test_payfast_itn_idempotency.py` (8 checks: first activation, exact redelivery no-op x2 fields, legitimate new-charge renewal x3 fields, exact redelivery of THAT second charge no-op x2 fields) - **8/8 PASS**. **Red:** identical test re-run against a second fresh 115-migration replay with `0125` itself excluded - **4/8 FAIL**, exactly the four no-op assertions (the two legitimate-renewal checks still passed, confirming the test isn't failing everything indiscriminately). **Green again:** real unmodified replay, 8/8 PASS.

**Regression check:** `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py` (`ALL PASSED`) and `engine/compliance/test_principals_registrations.py` (`0 failure(s)`) both re-run against the same 115-migration database this fix lives in - unaffected. **The bug, in one line.** `0128`'s own four new RESTRICTIVE policies on `storage.objects` for the `cv-documents` bucket share `cv_documents_path_person_id(name) is distinct from own_linked_person_id(...)` inside a `not(...)` wrapper. `IS DISTINCT FROM` treats two `null`s as NOT distinct (i.e. equal) - the opposite of ordinary `=`/`<>` null-propagation. `cv_documents_path_person_id()` returns `null` for ANY object name that doesn't parse to the exact `"<company>/people/<person>/<file>"` shape (by design, "never raises"); `own_linked_person_id()` returns `null` for an employee with no linked `people` row (also by design). When BOTH are null at once - an unlinked employee presenting any malformed/non-conventional path - `null IS DISTINCT FROM null` = `false`, so the policy's own deny branch never fires: full SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE on every malformed-path object in the bucket, bounded to their own company (the base `0008` tenant-isolation policy still holds; confirmed not a cross-tenant leak), but a genuine, severe bypass of the exact "employee restricted to own person" protection `0128` exists to add.

null`. But `migrations/0085_savings_counter.sql` created both backing columns as `numeric not null
default 20`/`numeric not null default 450` (confirmed directly: `grep -rln` across every migration

But found one genuinely new, concrete, cross-open-PR collision worth recording: `#188`'s and `#189`'s own `engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py` diffs each independently define a Python function named **`part2_storage_employee_gap(db)`** - byte-for-byte the same name - with completely different bodies (one tests `tender-documents`, the other `cv-documents`), each inserted at the identical point in the file and each wired into `main()` with an identical new call line in the identical place, neither PR aware the other exists. If both ever merge, Python's own name-rebinding semantics mean only the LAST definition in the merged file survives - the other bucket's entire regression test silently becomes dead code, called under its own name but running the wrong bucket's assertions, with no error anywhere. Widened the check across the whole six-PR storage family (`#188`-`#193`) and found a second, milder echo of the same unawareness: all six PRs (`#188` through `#193`) print their new Part-2 block under the identical human-readable index label `"[20]"` and all six insert their own new call in `main()` at the identical anchor line (right after `part2_team_billing_rpcs(Db(psql))`) - harmless for the four whose function NAMES are unique (`#190`/`#191`/`#192`/`#193` each use a distinct name), but a real, demonstrated duplicate-label/same-insertion-point hazard once more than one of the six merges. This is the same "two (here, six) open PRs share a surface, neither aware of the other" shape this segment has now found five times (`#186`'s NULL bug, `#187`/`#195`'s merge-order collision, `#176`'s lock regression, `#178`/`#180`'s fail-open gate), but this is the sharpest instance yet - an exact Python function-NAME collision, not just a shared primitive or a migration number. Documented-only below, per the standing precedent, since the bug lives only on two (more broadly, six) open, unmerged PR branches this review may not alter. Nothing pushed to any PR branch, no competing PR opened, no new `QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md` Finding number consumed (nothing here needed fixing on `main` or on a review-opened PR - every PR's own actual SQL fix is correct and independent; the collision is confined to the shared Python test harness file, which only becomes a live problem once two or more of these branches are merged together).

**The new finding: `#188` and `#189` define the byte-for-byte identical Python function name in
`engine/security/test_tenant_isolation.py`, each unaware the other exists - a sharper instance of
the cross-open-PR-collision shape than any found so far this segment.** Grepped every one of
`#188`-`#193`'s own diffs to this one file for `^\+def part2` and `print("\n\[`: `#188`'s own diff
defines `def part2_storage_employee_gap(db):` (testing `tender-documents`); `#189`'s own diff
ALSO defines `def part2_storage_employee_gap(db):` (testing `cv-documents`) - the identical name,
confirmed character-for-character by direct diff read of both, not a typo in this entry. Both
functions are inserted at the identical point in the file (immediately before `def main():`) and
both PRs' own `main()` diffs insert an identical new call line, `part2_storage_employee_gap(Db(psql))`,
in the identical place (immediately after the existing `part2_team_billing_rpcs(Db(psql))` line).
Neither PR's diff references the other PR at all - each was clearly written against the SAME
pre-`#188`/pre-`#189` `main`, independently, by an author (or review pass) choosing the same obvious
name for the same shape of test. **Why this matters, mechanically, if both ever merge**: Python
resolves a `def` by rebinding the module-level name at execution time - whichever of the two
`part2_storage_employee_gap` definitions appears LATER in the final merged file is the only one
that ever runs, under that name, for the rest of the file's life. The earlier one's own body
becomes syntactically present but semantically dead - never called, even though `main()` would then
contain the call line TWICE (once from each PR's own diff), both of which would simply invoke the
SAME surviving function, twice in a row. Concretely: whichever of `#188`/`#189` merges SECOND would
silently and permanently delete the OTHER PR's own regression coverage for its own bucket, with
`main()` reporting success (both calls return normally, both run the surviving function's
assertions, which all pass) and giving no indication anything is missing - the single most silent
failure mode this review's own technique exists to catch, here living in the TEST HARNESS itself
rather than in application code. This does not affect `main` today (neither PR is merged) and does
not affect the correctness of either PR's own actual SQL migration (`0127` vs `0128` are different,
non-colliding file numbers, and the underlying RLS fixes are fully independent and both individually
correct, as reproduced above) - it is confined entirely to a shared Python test file, and only
becomes a live problem the moment both branches are merged.

**A second, milder echo of the same unawareness across the WHOLE six-PR bucket family.** Widened
the same grep to all six storage-bucket PRs (`#188` through `#193`): every one of them - not just
`#188`/`#189` - prints its own new Part-2 block under the identical human-readable index label
`"[20]"` (`#188`: `tender-documents`; `#189`: `cv-documents`; `#190`: `company-documents`; `#191`:
`experience-documents`; `#192`: `submission-packs`; `#193`: `narrative-documents`/
`onboarding-documents`), and every one of them inserts its own new call in `main()` at the
identical anchor line, right after `part2_team_billing_rpcs(Db(psql))`. The other four
(`#190`/`#191`/`#192`/`#193`) each use a distinct, unique Python function NAME, so merging any
combination of those four (without `#188`/`#189`) would not silently drop any test - Python would
simply end up with six distinct functions, all genuinely called, all genuinely passing - but the
printed output would show up to six different, unrelated blocks all labelled `"[20]"`, a cosmetic
but real "whoever merges these should renumber the index labels by hand" hazard, and a second,
separate thing the eventual merger of this family needs to know regardless of the `#188`/`#189`
name collision.

**Recommendation for Sarel, documented-only, nothing pushed to any PR branch.** When merging any
two or more of `#188`-`#193`: (1) `#188` and `#189` specifically need one of their two
`part2_storage_employee_gap` functions renamed before or during the merge, or one's own test
coverage silently vanishes - this is not optional, it is a correctness requirement for the test
suite's own integrity, not a style nit; (2) whichever of the six merges in whatever order, the
survivor's own `"[20]"` print labels should be renumbered sequentially (`[20]`, `[21]`, `[22]`, ...)
for readable output, though this part is cosmetic only. No action needed on the four SQL fixes
themselves beyond the standing backlog note (merge-readiness aside, `#189`/`#190`/`#191`/`#192` are

**`#177` (`app/proxy.ts`, `company_members` read had no error capture) - read in full, clean, no
new issue.** The fix changes `const { data: membership } = await supabase.from("company_members")...`
to also capture `error: membershipError`, and changes the redirect-to-`/onboarding` gate from
`if (!membership && !path.startsWith("/onboarding"))` to `if (membershipError) { console.error(...) }
else if (!membership && ...) { redirect }` - on a transient read failure, falls through to the
real destination instead of a misleading `/onboarding` redirect. Checked whether "fall through on
error" is a fail-OPEN authorization gap (the exact shape this review hunts hardest for) by reading
every downstream consumer this proxy gate is the only thing standing in front of: `requireCompanyId()`
(`app/app/tenders/[id]/actions.ts`, confirmed identical pattern exists in all 15 `actions.ts` files
that define it) already re-reads `company_members` itself and explicitly fails closed on its OWN
read error (`if (membershipError) throw new Error("Couldn't verify your company - try again.")`,
confirmed by direct read, line 27) - so a Server Action reached via this fallthrough cannot act on
stale/wrong company data even if the proxy's own gate let the request through. For a page.tsx that
reads data directly rather than through an `actions.ts` function (checked `app/app/dashboard/
page.tsx`, which has zero `company_members`/`requireCompanyId` references of its own at all), the
actual tenant scoping is enforced by each table's own RLS policy (`is_company_member()`), not by
this proxy - a genuinely companyless user reaching `/dashboard` on a transient blip sees an empty/
RLS-scoped page, not another company's data. Concluded: this proxy check is a UX navigation
convenience, not the tenant-isolation boundary (RLS is), so falling open here on a transient error
is correct, matches the fix's own stated reasoning, and is NOT the same shape as `#178`'s own fail-
open bug (a real server-side hard-stop gate silently not firing) found two passes ago. **No bug
found.**

**Conclusion on Step 4: the preceding pass's own reasoning holds. RLS predicate NULL-handling is
genuinely, verifiably fail-CLOSED** (a `NULL` `using`/`with check` result denies the row/write, same
as `false` would) **- the OPPOSITE of the PL/pgSQL `IF <condition> THEN RAISE` fail-OPEN direction**
that made `0125`'s own `<>` a genuine bug (there, a `NULL` condition means the `RAISE` is skipped,
which is the one branch that was supposed to DENY access - so `NULL` there means "allowed through",
not "denied"). This is not a smaller version of the same risk living somewhere else; it is the
reason the SAME nullable helper (`own_linked_person_id()`) is safe to compare with a bare `=` in six

`generated_cvs`/`cv_extraction_results`/`person_role_eligibility`) and unsafe to compare with a bare
`<>` in exactly one place (`0125`'s own PL/pgSQL guard) - confirmed live in both directions this
pass, not re-derived from the operator alone.

  <boolean, never null>` has no NULL-handling surface at all. Clean.

  that is where the bug sits.
- **`0126` (PR #187, `record_tender_document_employee_gap`)** - `record_tender_document()`'s new
  guard is `if is_employee_in_company(v_company) then raise` - an outright block, same shape as

  needed the narrower per-person check at all: Tender Workspace is not one of an employee's two
  allowed pages, same reasoning the PR's own header gives.)
- **`0127`-`0133` (PRs #188-#193, the 7 storage-bucket employee-gap migrations: tender-documents,

  `experience-documents`/`submission-packs`/`narrative-documents`/`onboarding-documents`) use the
  same outright-exclude shape (`is_employee_in_company((storage.foldername(name))[1]::uuid)` ANDed

  person (`cv_documents_path_person_id()` = that person's real, non-null id), `<real-uuid> IS

**The bug, in full - `apply_my_cv_extraction_checked()` (PR #186's own `0125`):**

```sql
if is_employee_in_company(v_company_id) and p_person_id <> own_linked_person_id(v_company_id) then
  raise exception 'That extraction result wasn''t found for you.' using errcode = '42501';
end if;
```

`own_linked_person_id(p_company_id)` (0077) is `select id from people where company_id =
p_company_id and linked_user_id = auth.uid()` - it returns `null`, not an error, when the signed-in
user has no linked `people` row in this company at all. Its own 0077 comment says outright: "or
null if they have none (e.g. an owner/admin/member who was never linked to a person...)" - but an
`employee`-role member can be in exactly this state too, and nothing in the schema prevents it:
`create_company_invite_checked(p_company_id, p_email, p_role, p_linked_person_id)` (0113) takes
`p_linked_person_id` as a plain, nullable parameter with no constraint tying it to `p_role`, and
`redeem_company_invite()` (0077) joins `company_members` with the invite's own `role` unconditionally
- it only attempts the `people.linked_user_id` link `if v_invite.linked_person_id is not null`,
skipping that step entirely otherwise. So inviting someone as `role = 'employee'` with
`p_linked_person_id = null` - a completely ordinary admin action, needing no special tooling - leaves
that employee with `own_linked_person_id()` permanently `null` until someone links a person to them
by hand.

When that happens, `p_person_id <> null` evaluates to SQL `NULL` (not `true`/`false`) for ANY
`p_person_id`, so `is_employee_in_company(...) and NULL` is `NULL` whenever the employee check is
true. PL/pgSQL's `IF <condition> THEN` treats a `NULL` condition exactly like `false` - the `raise
exception` branch is silently skipped, not entered - and execution falls straight through to the
function's own pre-existing checks (`v_row_person_id <> p_person_id`, `v_status <> 'pending_review'`),
both of which the attacker can trivially satisfy by naming a real, pending colleague extraction. The
write proceeds in full.

**Reproduced red, independently, in a fresh scratch Postgres** (`engine/security/replay_schema.sh`
against `main`'s real 113 migrations, then PR `#186`'s own `0125` applied on top via `git show
origin/pr/186:app/supabase/migrations/0125_cv_extraction_apply_employee_gap.sql | psql` - never `main`
itself, never a different PR's content mixed in). Seeded one company; one `owner`; one `employee`
member with **zero** `people` rows linking to them at all (the state above); one separate `people`
row for a colleague, never linked to any account; one `cv_uploads` + `pending_review`
`cv_extraction_results` row for that colleague. Acting as the employee (`set role authenticated;
select set_config('test.uid', '<employee uuid>', true)`):
- Sanity check first: `select is_employee_in_company('<company>')` -> `t`; `select
  own_linked_person_id('<company>')` -> empty/`null` - confirmed directly, not assumed from the
  schema alone.
- `select apply_my_cv_extraction_checked('<colleague's extraction id>', '<colleague's person id>',
  '{"phone":"9999999999","name":"PWNED BY EMPLOYEE WITH NO LINKED PERSON"}', '{}')` - **SUCCEEDED**,
  no error.
- A follow-up superuser read confirmed the colleague's real `people.name`/`people.phone` had been
  overwritten to the attacker-supplied values, and `cv_extraction_results.review_status` was now
  `'applied'` with `reviewed_by` set to the ATTACKING EMPLOYEE's own uid - a full, unrestricted
  read/write bypass of a colleague's record by an employee who, by the fix's own stated intent, was
  supposed to be confined to "their OWN linked person" and nothing else.

**Confirmed green with the exact, minimal, NULL-safe fix** (`IS DISTINCT FROM` in place of `<>`,

**This pass's own task, per the standing brief: grep every Server Action's plain `.update(`/`.insert(`/
`.delete(` through the user's own RLS-bound `createClient()` and, for each target table, confirm
against the table's OWN migration SQL (never assumed from a sibling) that a real PERMISSIVE policy
grants that exact operation to `authenticated` - the lesson Finding 201/PR #184 proved: a missing grant
is a structural bug no race-focused check would ever catch.**

**Method: not just the five named candidate tables - a full, codebase-wide grant map, built once and
cross-referenced against every write site.** Wrote a small parser (kept in this pass's own scratchpad,
not committed - it's a throwaway grep aid, not product code) that reads every
`app/supabase/migrations/*.sql` file in order and extracts every `create policy ... for <op> to <role>
...` statement (PERMISSIVE and RESTRICTIVE separately; `for all` expands to all four CRUD ops), to get
one authoritative "which operations does `authenticated` actually hold on this table" answer per table
- a later migration that drops and re-declares a table's policies (exactly what 0026 did to
`pack_generation_jobs`, below) is reflected automatically rather than relying on remembering which
migration is the "current" one for a given table. Cross-referenced that map against
`grep -rn "\.from(\"<table>\")" app/app --include="*.ts*" | grep -v spec` for every table whose
authenticated grant was NOT the full `['select','insert','update','delete']` set, reading each actual
call site to see which operation it performs and whether that operation is in the table's own granted
set.

read individually, not inferred from the table's shape:**

**The one genuine, previously-undocumented structural asymmetry found: `pack_generation_jobs`'s own
engine-split grant (migration 0026) - but every real write site already routes around it correctly, so
this is a negative, not a new Finding.** 0017's original policy granted `authenticated` members full
CRUD (`for all ... using (is_company_member(company_id))`). 0026 (introducing the unified `sanral`/
`general` job queue) **dropped that policy and replaced it with four narrower ones**: members can
select any of their own company's rows; members can insert a `requested` row of EITHER engine; members
can update a SANRAL-engine row; members can delete a SANRAL-engine row. **A `general`-engine row -
every non-SANRAL requirement-extraction/pack job - has only SELECT and INSERT; no authenticated UPDATE
or DELETE grant exists for it at all** - structurally the same shape as `onboarding_uploads`/Finding
201, just split by a `engine` column instead of being table-wide. 0026's own migration comment already
flags half of this ("nothing in the app uses [update/delete on SANRAL rows] today") but does not flag
the general-engine gap by name.

Read every Server Action that can reach this table to see whether any of them assumes the missing
grant: `tenders/[id]/actions.ts`'s `requestSubmissionPack()` (SANRAL) inserts via
`request_submission_pack_checked()`, a `security definer` RPC - never a plain `.insert()`.
`tenders/[id]/general-actions.ts`'s `requestJob()` (both `requestRequirementsExtraction()` and
`requestGeneralPack()`, general-engine) inserts via `request_general_job_checked()` - same pattern.
`removePrivateTenderDocument()`'s own re-queue-after-removing-a-document branch (same file, line ~323)
also goes through `request_general_job_checked()`, not a direct insert. `admin/requirement-extractions/
actions.ts`'s `reprocessRequirementExtraction()` goes through `platform_admin_reprocess_requirement_
extraction()`. Every other reference to this table in `app/app` (`activity-log.tsx`, `submission-
pack.tsx`, `sanral-schedules/page.tsx`, `intake-card.tsx`'s `tender_engine_jobs` read) is a plain
`.select()`. **No Server Action anywhere does a bare `.update()`/`.delete()` on this table, SANRAL or
general** - the gap this pass found in the grant itself has nothing in the app that could ever hit it.
Logged here, not as a new Finding, precisely so a future pass doesn't need to re-derive this same
grant-map question for this table - the grant asymmetry is real and worth knowing about structurally,
but there is no bug to fix behind it today.

**Is this angle exhausted?** Not entirely - this pass covered the full set of tables whose authenticated
grant is anything less than full CRUD (29 tables total, listed above plus the 5 named candidates), cross-

**Lead (`people/actions.ts`'s `retryCvExtraction()` and `document-scan/actions.ts`'s
`retryOnboardingUpload()`, around line 486) - read both in full, re-derived rather than trusted the
prior pass's own characterization, and found one real correction to it: genuine negative for both,
but for two different reasons.**

Both do the identical shape: a 3-`.eq()` (`id`/`company_id`/status-guard) `.update()` with no
`.select()` at all, so a zero-row match (an RLS race, or the row having already moved off the
guarded status) produces `error: null` and is indistinguishable from a real update by `error`
alone.

`retryCvExtraction()` (`app/app/people/actions.ts`) redirects to `/people/${personId}` with **no**
`?saved=`/`?error=` param either way on this path - confirmed by reading the function to its last
line, not assumed. A zero-row match therefore changes nothing observable: the page re-renders
whatever the row's TRUE current status actually is (via `revalidatePath`), which is exactly what
the user should see regardless of whether this particular click caused it. No path in this file
deletes a `cv_uploads` row either (only `deletePerson()`'s own cascade does, a generic
concurrent-delete race shared by every action on this page, not specific to this zero-row shape).

`document-scan/actions.ts`'s `retryOnboardingUpload()` does **not** match the prior pass's own
characterization - re-reading it line by line found it actually redirects `${back}?saved=retrying`
on success, which `page.tsx`'s own `SAVED` map renders as "Queued again - this page updates itself
as the result comes in." - a real, user-visible toast the prior pass's description missed. That
matters, because it means a zero-row match here CAN surface a "success" toast with no matching
write; the real question is whether that toast is ever actually false. Traced every path that can
move `onboarding_uploads.status` away from `classification_failed`: `engine/onboarding/
process_onboarding_jobs.py`'s own worker and its stale-`classifying`-row reclaim logic (lines
~98-142) never touch a `classification_failed` row at all - only rows already in `classifying` get
reclaimed. The ONLY write that can ever move a row OFF `classification_failed` is this same action.
So the only way to reach a zero-row match here is two submissions of the same retry racing each
other (a double-click, two tabs, or two users) - Postgres's own row-level locking means exactly one
of two concurrent `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'classification_failed'` statements actually matches
and moves the row; the other sees `status != 'classification_failed'` and matches zero rows, with
no error. Both callers still land on the "retrying" toast - but the document genuinely IS being
retried in that case, just caused by the other click, not this one. There is no `onboarding_uploads`
row-delete path anywhere in this file (confirmed by grep - no `.delete()` on this table in
`document-scan/actions.ts`), so there's no "retry an already-deleted upload" variant of this race to
worry about either. The toast's own copy hedges exactly this ("this page updates itself as the
result comes in") rather than asserting a fact only this specific click could have caused.
**Genuine negative for both functions, for two different reasons** - logged here rather than
`QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md` (there's no fix to anchor a Finding number to) so a future pass doesn't
need to re-open this exact question, and so the `?saved=retrying` correction above isn't lost.

**Found: Finding 191.** Reading the two "confirm this AI-extracted CV" Server Actions side by side -
not just how each one gets to its own locked rpc call (already fixed, identical shape on both), but
what each one does AFTER that rpc succeeds - `applyCvExtraction()` (`people/actions.ts`, the full
People page) calls `queueStandardCvs()` right after; `applyMyCvExtraction()` (`my-cv/actions.ts`, the
My CV self-service page, 0065's `employee` role) does not call it, or anything equivalent, at all.
`queueStandardCvs()` was the ONLY writer anywhere in this codebase of a `generated_cvs` row with
`tender_id` null (confirmed by grep - no second writer exists), and both confirm rpcs require the
extraction's own `review_status` to still be `'pending_review'`, so a CV confirmed exclusively through
My CV never got its 4 standard CV formats queued, with literally no way for anyone - including an
owner/admin on the full People page - to ever trigger it for that same extraction again. Real
consumers, confirmed by reading each one, not assumed: both the My CV page's and the full People
page's own "My generated CVs (read-only)" cards (`is("tender_id", null)`) showed "None generated yet."
permanently; `engine/general/process_general_jobs.py`'s own per-role `generated_cvs` lookup in
`gather()` (no `tender_id` filter - takes the newest `ready` row for a person, standard or
tender-specific, as a real fallback CV source for general-tender packs) would show "no CV uploaded or
generated for this person" for a person whose CV was, in fact, fully confirmed, if no tender-specific
CV or as-is upload existed for them.

**Fix**: extracted `queueStandardCvs()` out of `people/actions.ts` into a new shared
`app/lib/standardCvQueue.ts`, and called it from `applyMyCvExtraction()` right after its own rpc
succeeds - `requireOwnPerson()` already returns `userId`/`companyId` alongside `personId`, so no new

  row is `error_message: null` by construction from the moment it's inserted, on both engines, so
  general's missing reset can never actually observe a stale value. Genuine negative, not a gap with a
  reachable consequence.

  dir=work_root)`) - the one real candidate for "SANRAL stores something general deliberately doesn't."

  downstream consumer" bar requires, rather than stopping at "it's in the JSONB column": (1)

  members `select` their own rows directly - so in principle a signed-in company member's browser

  entirely; (2) grepped every real `.from("pack_generation_jobs")` call site in `app/app`
  (`actions.ts`, `activity-log.tsx`, `submission-pack.tsx`, `sanral-schedules/page.tsx`) and read each:
  only `submission-pack.tsx` selects the `manifest` column at all, and its own `PackJob["manifest"]`

  `financial`) - but a TS type annotation doesn't strip extra runtime keys, so this alone doesn't prove
  anything; (3) traced where that fetched row data actually goes: `j.manifest.warnings`,
  `checklistOf(j.manifest)` (-> `j.manifest.checklist`/`.sections`/`.omitted` only, confirmed by reading
  `checklistOf()` in `pack-checklist.tsx`) - `PackChecklist` (the only component these feed) is **not**

  prop; `DownloadAllButton` (the one real `"use client"` component on this page) receives only
  `urls: string[]` (pre-computed signed URLs), never `j.manifest` itself. **The raw `manifest` object,

  identical shape. **Conclusion: a real inconsistency (general was deliberately narrowed to 8 keys at

   number, every teammate's email, and could also trigger real paid actions (request a tender pack,
   consuming quota) on the company's behalf. Fixed by adding the same role check these functions'
   own sibling tables already have. Clean against `main`, clean against every other open PR. Biggest
   single PR in the batch (830 lines) but every one of the 12 fixes is the identical one-line-guard
   pattern, each individually tested both ways (employee blocked, owner/member unaffected).
2. **#182 - "Two more places with the exact same employee-data-leak bug #176 just found - these two
   got missed."** Same story as #176, just 2 functions instead of 12 (both about how many tender
   packs a company has used/can still request). Small, clean, independent of #176 either way.
3. **#183 - "If someone double-clicks 'Confirm' on an onboarding document (or has the same screen
   open in two tabs), the same document can get filed twice - duplicating real records."** The
   direct follow-on to the fix already on `main` (commit `1a65a86`) for the exact same bug on a
   different screen (CV extraction). This PR covers onboarding's own "confirm this scanned document"
   screen (company registration doc, ID document, a reference letter, a CV handoff) - 6 different
   buttons sharing one unguarded check. Clean against everything else. Largest diff after #176 (597
   lines) because each of the 4 riskiest confirm buttons needs its own small database lock, not one
   shared fix.
4. **#181 - "The automatic 'Your tender pack is ready' email has never actually been sent, for
   any company, since the feature launched on 27 October - found by finding the bug, not by seeing
   it fail."** The email-sending code needs a tool (`node`) that was simply never installed in the
   production worker, and the one file it needs was explicitly excluded from what gets shipped to
   production - so every attempt fails silently and the error gets swallowed into an internal log
   nobody but a session like this one reads. This PR installs the missing tool and un-excludes the
   one file genuinely needed (not the whole app). **This is the only one of the 10 PRs with a real,
   passing CI run on its exact code** (a manually-triggered build-and-test run, green). Isolated to
   2 files (a Dockerfile and a `.dockerignore`), clean against everything else - but it is a change
   to what ships inside the production worker's container image, which is why it's worth a human
   glance even though it's narrow.
5. **#178 + #180 - merge together, not #178 alone (they conflict with each other and are two
   halves of one fix).** #178: the "Fix N items before you can submit" rule was only ever enforced
   by greying out a button in the browser - nothing stopped a direct request from actually building
   and sending a non-compliant submission pack. This closes that gap on the server, for both tender
   types. #180: separately, when the system can't tell if everything's actually fixed (a temporary
   read hiccup), it was wrongly treating "couldn't check" as "all clear" in 3 different places
   (the Submit button, a pipeline status badge, and the "are you still impersonating someone"
   warning banner) - this makes all 3 fail safe instead. #180's own description says plainly that if
   #178 merges without it, #178's new server-side check inherits that exact same "couldn't check =
   assume it's fine" gap. **They touch the same 2 files in a way Git cannot auto-merge** - whoever
   merges these should merge #180 first, then manually re-apply #178's own change on top (both diffs
   are short and readable), rather than trying to merge #178 alone.
6. **#179 - "Reusing a past submission as a starting point for a new tender never checked whether
   the tender you're copying it ONTO has already been submitted - only whether the one you're
   copying FROM was valid."** A stale browser tab or a replayed request could silently overwrite the
   answers on a tender that's already gone in to the buyer. Real, worth having - but **this PR
   currently conflicts with `main` itself** (a different, already-merged fix touched the exact same
   line) and needs a small rebase before it's even mergeable; recommend asking for that rebase
   before spending a review cycle on it.
7. **#177 (draft) - "A blip in the login-gate check was wrongly treated as 'this person has no
   company yet' and bounced them to the signup screen instead of wherever they were actually going."**
   Runs on every single page load for every signed-in user, so it's the widest-blast-radius fix in
   the batch, but the change itself can only ever produce *fewer* wrong redirects, never more (by
   the PR author's own careful reasoning, re-confirmed by reading the diff directly: it only adds an
   extra "was this actually an error?" condition before redirecting). Small (1 file, 19 lines),
   clean against everything else. Still marked draft - worth flipping out of draft before/at merge
   time, no code reason to wait.
8. **#164 and #165 - oldest two PRs (opened 2026-10-26, ~12 days ago), both still draft, and both

   the files it touches, this one most needs Sarel's own judgment call: redo it against current
   `main`, or confirm the underlying feature decision still stands before anyone spends the rebase

**This pass's angle, per the task brief: a SEVENTH systematic angle, applying the Finding-178/180
"unlocked read-then-write" / "TOCTOU gate bypass" lesson (previously found only in SQL) to
TypeScript Server Actions instead** - `app/app/*/actions.ts` and `app/lib/**` write-path helpers,
looking for (a) a read feeding a computed value into a write with no optimistic-concurrency guard
and no backing DB constraint/lock, or (b) a gate-check read followed by a SEPARATE write that never
re-checks the gate, where two genuinely concurrent invocations of the SAME Server Action (two tabs,
a double-click, two team members) could race.

**Method.** Read every `actions.ts` under `app/app/` (22 files: `admin/*`, `company/*`, `discovery`,
`experience`, `invite`, `my-cv`, `onboarding`, `people`, `pipeline`, `tenders/[id]`, `tenders/new`,
`_components`), tracing each write-after-read sequence into its real backing Postgres call (not
just reading the TypeScript in isolation) to tell which already inherit atomicity from a locked RPC
or a DB-level constraint and which don't.

**Already safe, checked and ruled out, each for a named reason:**
- `app/app/company/team/actions.ts` - `createInvite()`/`setMemberRole()`/`removeMember()` each
  already call a locked, checked RPC (`create_company_invite_checked` 0113,
  `set_member_role_checked`/`remove_member_checked` 0114) - their own header comments document the
  exact race this angle looks for, already closed by a prior pass.
- `app/app/company/bank-accounts/actions.ts` - `saveBankAccount()`'s write is a plain `.update()`/
  `.insert()` keyed by the form's own `id`/fields, not by a prior read's computed value; uniqueness
  is a real DB constraint (`bank_accounts_one_...`), not an app-level check-then-write. No TOCTOU
  gate read precedes either write.
- `app/app/tenders/[id]/actions.ts` `requestTenderCv()` - has an app-level "already pending?" SELECT
  before its INSERT, but migration 0075's partial unique index
  (`generated_cvs_dedupe_pending_idx`, scoped to `tender_pack_id is not null`) is the real,
  already-documented backstop: a race past the SELECT hits the unique index and returns a clean
  `23505`, handled explicitly. Not a candidate (same class Finding 178's own pass ruled
  `set_opportunity_interest()` out for).
- `app/app/discovery/actions.ts` - every write goes through `set_opportunity_tag()`/
  `set_opportunity_interest()`, already fixed/ruled-out by Finding 178's own migration 0121.
- `app/app/invite/actions.ts` - `redeem_company_invite()` RPC, already fixed by migration 0107/0122
  (Findings 180/the `redeem_company_invite` race).
- `app/app/people/actions.ts` `discardCvExtraction()` and `app/app/my-cv/actions.ts`
  `discardMyCvExtraction()` - both already guard their own update with
  `.eq("review_status", "pending_review")` (standing review, 2026-11-06), so a second concurrent
  discard (or a discard racing an apply) gets a clean zero-row "already moved on" error, not a
  silent double-discard.
- `app/app/pipeline/actions.ts`, `app/app/experience/actions.ts`, `app/app/company/principals|
  properties|registrations/actions.ts`, `app/app/onboarding/actions.ts`, `app/app/tenders/new/
  actions.ts`, `app/app/admin/*/actions.ts` - every write in these files is a plain `.update()`/
  `.insert()`/`.delete()` keyed directly by an id the caller supplied (or a freshly-generated one),
  never by a value read-then-recomputed from an earlier SELECT in the same request. No read-then-
  write window to race in the first place.

**The real finding: `applyCvExtraction()` (`app/app/people/actions.ts`) and its self-service twin
`applyMyCvExtraction()` (`app/app/my-cv/actions.ts`) both had exactly the angle-(b) shape - a gate-
check read, then a separate write that never re-checks the gate.** Both read `cv_extraction_results`
once, check `review_status === 'pending_review'`, then perform the people update / (for the full
version) projects insert / cv_extraction_results mark-applied write as **three separate, unlocked
REST calls**, and the LAST of those three never repeated the `review_status = 'pending_review'`
check in its own `.eq()` chain. Their own sibling, `discardMyCvExtraction()`/`discardCvExtraction()`,
already had exactly that guard (standing review, 2026-11-06, with a comment literally naming "the
row having moved on from 'pending_review' already" as the risk) - the two "apply" paths never got
it, a plain oversight: the fix landed on the sibling function, never the twin right next to it.

**Real, reachable race, not contrived:** two concurrent "Apply"/"Save selected fields" submissions
for the SAME extraction - a double-click before the page navigates away, or the same pending-review
card left open in two browser tabs - both pass the initial read's `review_status` check before
either commits. For `applyCvExtraction()` specifically this duplicates real rows in `projects` (NOT
idempotent - every ticked project gets inserted twice, silently, with no error to either caller) and
queues a second full set of standard-CV-generation jobs (`queueStandardCvs()`, itself already
flagged by its own comment as having no database-level backstop of its own, unlike
`requestTenderCv()`'s migration-0075-backed dedupe). Neither caller sees any error either way -
`cv_extraction_results.applied` is simply overwritten a second time and both redirects report
success.

**Fix (migration `0123_cv_extraction_apply_race.sql`), same pattern as 0121/0113/0107/0114: move the
read-gate-write sequence into one locked SQL transaction per caller.** `apply_cv_extraction_checked()`
and `apply_my_cv_extraction_checked()` (both `security definer`) lock the `cv_extraction_results` row
(`for update`), re-check company membership/person match/`review_status = 'pending_review'` under
that lock, then perform the people update (`_apply_cv_person_fields()`, a private, never-granted
helper mirroring the TypeScript `personUpdate` object's own "only ticked keys present" shape
exactly - same convention as 0024's `_manual_tender_documents()`), the projects insert (full version
only), and the mark-applied write, all before releasing the lock. A second concurrent call for the
SAME extraction blocks on the row lock until the first commits, then raises a clear error
("These extracted fields were already saved or discarded.") instead of silently re-applying. Both
Server Actions now make ONE `supabase.rpc()` call in place of their old three-separate-write
sequence; all validation (date format, select options, required fields, the SAST-anchored
`source_note`) stays exactly where it was, in TypeScript - only the WRITE itself moved into the
database.

**Verification - real two-session Postgres reproduction, not just unit tests.** Built a disposable
scratch database (`tt_scratch_0123`, local Postgres 16, started and stopped for this pass only,
dropped at the end - never this app's live DB) with a minimal schema matching the real
`companies`/`company_members`/`is_company_member()`/`people`/`projects`/`cv_uploads`/

`psql` sessions against the SAME extraction - both calls returned successfully, final `projects`
row count: **2** (the same project duplicated), `cv_extraction_results.applied` overwritten twice,
no error either side - the exact bug, reproduced for real. **Green:** the identical two concurrent
calls against `apply_cv_extraction_checked()` (a `pg_sleep(1)`-widened copy, to prove the second
caller genuinely BLOCKS rather than just winning a fast race - confirmed by wall-clock timing, the
second call's total time ~1.8s against the lock-wait + its own 1s sleep): the first call committed
normally (1 project row, ~0.56ms wait); the second call's `for update` blocked until the first
committed, then raised "These extracted fields were already saved or discarded." - final `projects`

date field) write correctly, a ticked project inserts correctly, `applied` metadata is stored
correctly, a second synchronous call on an already-applied row raises cleanly, and
`apply_my_cv_extraction_checked()` (no-projects variant) updates its one ticked field correctly.
Scratch DB dropped and the Postgres service stopped at the end of this pass.

**A second, real, CONCRETELY CHECKED (not speculative) instance of the exact same bug class, found
by this pass's own survey but deliberately NOT fixed this pass - named precisely for whoever opens
it next.** `app/app/company/document-scan/actions.ts` (483 lines, the onboarding AI-document-review
screen, 0063) has the identical angle-(b) shape, repeated across FIVE separate "confirm" paths that
all share one gate (`loadPendingResult()`, line 134: reads `onboarding_document_results`, checks
`review_status === 'pending_review'`) and one shared "mark applied" write (`markApplied()`, line
149: `update({review_status: 'applied', ...}).eq('id', resultId)` - no re-check of `review_status`
in its own `.eq()` chain, same gap `applyCvExtraction()` had). The clearest, most severe instance:
**`confirmExperienceItem()` (line ~291, `supabase.from("experience_items").insert(row)`)** - two
concurrent confirms of the SAME onboarding document (double-click, two tabs) would both pass
`loadPendingResult()`'s gate and both insert, producing a genuine duplicate `experience_items` row
with no error to either caller - the exact `projects`-duplication shape this pass's own fix just
closed for `cv_extraction_results`/`projects`. `confirmCvHandoff()` (line ~378,
`cv_uploads.insert()`) has the same duplicate-row risk; `confirmVaultDocument()` (line 226,
`companies.update()`) and `confirmIdDocument()` (line 339, `company_principals.update()`) are lower
severity (overwriting the same scalar columns twice is closer to idempotent, though each also
copies the source file to a FRESH `randomUUID()` path per call, so the loser's copy becomes a real,
silently orphaned file in storage - a cost/clutter leak, not corruption). `skipOnboardingDocument()`
(line 416) and `discardOnboardingDocument()` (line 444) already have a `.select("id").maybeSingle()`
zero-row check (2026-11-06 pass) but THAT check only catches an RLS-revocation race, not this one -
neither re-checks `review_status = 'pending_review'` in its own `.eq()` chain either, so a confirm
racing a discard/skip for the same document can leave `review_status` as whichever write committed
last, inconsistent with what was actually filed.

**Why this was found but NOT fixed this pass, deliberately:** unlike `cv_extraction_results`\
`'`s single shared target shape (people + projects, one RPC per caller), this file's fix needs a
SEPARATE locked RPC per confirm path (each writes a DIFFERENT target table - `companies`,
`experience_items`, `company_principals`, `cv_uploads` - plus a storage-copy side effect each), and
merely guarding `markApplied()`'s own final write (the ".eq() alone is sufficient" option) would
NOT close the real race, for the same reason it wouldn't have for `applyCvExtraction()`: the
damaging write (the insert/update) happens BEFORE `markApplied()` runs, so by the time a guard on
the last step could reject the loser, the duplicate insert has already happened. A correct fix
needs the SAME "lock the gate row before the first dependent write, not just the last one" pattern
this pass's own `0123` migration establishes, applied five separate times with equal care (and,
ideally, five separate real two-session reproductions) - a properly-scoped pass of its own, not a
rushed addition to this one. Flagged here with exact file/line evidence so a future pass can open it
directly rather than re-discovering it from scratch.

**Following that duplication one level deeper surfaced the real, bigger bug.** If
`fetch_documents()` worked correctly, RFP18/2026's "What's New" document links would be fully
redundant with its own detail page, by design (both link the same 3 documents). Running the real,
unmodified `fetch_documents()` against the real live detail-page HTML for BOTH of SARS's 2
currently open tenders (RFP14/2026, RFP18/2026) returned **`[]` for both** - zero documents,
including the tender's own primary "advert"/specification pack, not just a later addendum. Root
cause, read directly off the real HTML: SARS's WordPress site links every tender document through
a pretty permalink with NO file extension in the URL at all (e.g. "/rfp18-2026-tender-pack/",
confirmed 301-redirecting server-side to the real `.pdf` via `curl -L -v`) - `DOC_LINK`'s own regex,
requiring the href to literally END in a file extension, matched zero of them. This has been true
since this reader's first commit (`cace3f7`): every SARS tender ever discovered has had its own
real documents silently recorded as empty, contradicting `download_discovered_documents.py`'s own
docstring, which wrongly asserts this source "gives a direct, unauthenticated link" the same way
the other 7 sources genuinely do. The only existing test for `fetch_documents()` used a synthetic
fixture with hrefs already ending in `.pdf` - never checked against the real site's actual URL
shape, which is why this went undetected through every prior pass that touched this file. A second,
compounding gap found the same way: RFP18/2026's own real "Main" tender-pack link text reuses the

extension-agnostic fix alone would still have missed it.

structure: every document link sits inside the post's own single `elementor-widget-theme-post-
content` widget, under a `<p><strong>Main</strong></p>` marker (optionally followed by `<p><strong>
Supporting</strong></p>` and more links). New `_DOC_SECTION` regex scopes to exactly that one
widget's own container (stopping at its first closing `</div>`) - deliberately NOT a page-wide
match, since the page's shared nav/footer chrome ("Home"/"About SARS"/"Careers"/...) is ALSO a
plain extension-less `https://www.sars.gov.za/...` link; matching page-wide would have swept all of
that in as bogus "documents". New `_SECTION_LINK` regex (no title-length cap, safe since it only
ever runs against this small, already-scoped section) extracts every real link inside it.
`fetch_documents()` now merges `DOC_LINK`'s matches (kept, unchanged, in case a raw file link ever
appears again) with the new section match, de-duplicated by resolved URL exactly as before.

  concurrency; nothing to race against a second call of a function that doesn't exist at runtime.

  `t`'s stale snapshot. This is exactly the safe shape 0121's own fix converged on (the append
  expression evaluated under the row's own lock at write time) - genuinely clean, not a near-miss.

  `update discovered_opportunities set tender_id = t_id where id = opp.id` - re-verified against
  this pass's own stricter "could a concurrent call silently clobber a value" test, not just
  reread: both writes are naturally idempotent (the tenders upsert only ever bumps `last_seen_at`
  from a fresh `now()`, never from a stale field of `opp`; the `tender_id` write derives from

  conclusion for `set_opportunity_interest()`, now re-confirmed for this function too rather than
  assumed.

  update`) WOULD have had a genuine TOCTOU race - two different companies' concurrent first uploads

  own data. Confirmed via `grep -n "record_tender_document" app/app/tenders/[id]/pack-inputs-
  actions.ts` that the app still calls the same RPC name/signature the current (safe) version

- `0048`/`0106`/`0111`'s three successive versions of `accept_tender_update_date()` already had

- No `col +/- n` arithmetic read-then-write pattern found anywhere in the 111 migration files
  (checked with a separate regex for `count`/`quantity`/`balance`/`credits`/`used`/`remaining`/

anything on this read's failure, so this is a real display-only miss, not the dominant bug class.

**Found a real one - Finding 168, reported, deliberately NOT fixed this pass.** Full write-up:
Finding 168 in `docs/specs/QA-Edge-Case-Findings.md`. One-line summary: `company_packs_this_period()`
(`0115_pack_quota_regression_and_request_race.sql`) counts every pack requested since `company_
subscriptions.current_period_start` with no monthly re-derivation at all, and `current_period_start`
is only ever reset by a successful PayFast ITN (`apply_payfast_itn()`, `0112`) - which for a
`billing_interval = 'yearly'` company fires roughly once a YEAR (`lib/payfast.ts`'s own
`PAYFAST_FREQUENCY`: monthly=3, yearly=6), not once a month. But `max_packs_per_month` is explicitly,
by name and by `lib/billing.ts`'s own header comment, a MONTHLY allowance, identical whether a
company pays monthly or pays the same rate annually up front. Net effect: a yearly-billing company
that uses its full monthly allotment once, early in its 12-month cycle, stays capped at that same
count and blocked from requesting any more packs for the remaining ~11 months, instead of getting a
fresh monthly allotment every month like a monthly-billing company on the identical plan gets. This
is a severe UNDER-grant (roughly 1/12th the real annual volume for the same money), not an over-
grant, but it is exactly the "billing-period-boundary bug" shape the brief asked about.

**Live-reproduced in a disposable scratch Postgres** (`service postgresql start`; `su postgres -c
"psql -c 'CREATE DATABASE scratch_quota168'"`; `engine/security/replay_schema.sh -U postgres -d
scratch_quota168`, all 110 migrations applied clean; dropped and `service postgresql stop`
afterward - nothing left running). Seeded a yearly Professional company (`max_packs_per_month=15`,
`current_period_start` 11 months ago, `current_period_end` 1 month away - the ordinary middle of a
yearly cycle) with exactly 15 `ready` `pack_generation_jobs` rows dated to month 1 of that period
(its real, full, legitimately-used monthly allotment, used once, 11 months back, nothing since). As
that company's own `owner`: `company_packs_this_period()` returned **15** (should be 0 - nothing
requested in the current calendar month), `company_can_request_pack()` returned **false** (should be
true), and the real live gate, `request_general_job_checked(..., 'generate_pack')`, **raised** the
exact user-facing "You've reached your plan's bid pack limit for this period..." error a real
customer would hit 11 months into a 12-month cycle having requested nothing in 11 months. Full
reproduction steps (exact SQL) are in Finding 168's own write-up.

**Why reported, not fixed or PR'd, this pass - the brief's own explicit caution, not a shortcut.**
The right SQL fix requires Sarel to pick a semantics for "this period" on a yearly plan (an
anniversary-day-aligned rolling monthly window, a plain calendar-month window, or treating a yearly
plan's allowance as `max_packs_per_month * 12` up front) - a product-policy call, not a QA one, the
same shape of decision the standing guardrail already reserves for `start_payfast_checkout()`'s own
revenue-integrity gap (2026-11-07e). This finding is about a DIFFERENT function (`company_packs_
this_period()`, not `start_payfast_checkout()`) and does not touch or implement any part of that
guarded item - the standing guardrail against touching `start_payfast_checkout()`'s fix was not
breached, just the same "ask Sarel, don't guess on money-adjacent semantics" judgment applied to a
sibling function.

## This pass (2026-11-07w, standing solution-architect review): independently re-verified the
sibling track's `0f6595b` ("~46 SECURITY DEFINER functions' revoke-from-public never actually
removed anon's own execute grant", migration `0120`) against primary sources, not assertion - every
claim in it checks out. No new bug found or fixed by this pass; this entry exists because a
significant security claim from a track this chain hadn't independently checked deserved the same
scrutiny this review applies to its own work before being treated as settled.

Oriented from `389d6a7` (this chain's own immediately-preceding pass, HEAD at that commit, matching
the verified HEAD this pass was given). `git fetch origin main`: clean, `origin/main` matched local

(`draft: false`), `#164`/`#165`/`#177` still drafts - all 8 unchanged, none merged or closed this
pass. No PR was touched, amended or merged.

**What was actually checked, with real evidence, not a re-read of the commit's own prose:**

1. **The underlying mechanism claim** (`alter default privileges in schema public grant all on
   functions to anon, ...` runs once, platform-side, separately from and untouched by `revoke all
   ... from public`) - confirmed this is pre-existing project infrastructure, not something the
   sibling commit invented to support its own narrative: `engine/security/scratch_supabase_stub.sql`
   already carried this exact `alter default privileges ... grant all on functions to anon,
   authenticated, service_role` line (`git log` on the file: last touched `abcd91f`, well before
   `0f6595b`/`fdf51d7`). This is standard, correct PostgreSQL behaviour (a named-role default-
   privilege grant and the generic `PUBLIC`-pseudo-role default are two independent ACL entries;
   revoking one never touches the other) - not a novel or dubious claim.

2. **The "52 anon-executable pre-fix" count** - reproduced for real. Started a real scratch
   Postgres 16 (`pg_ctlcluster 16 main start`, `sudo -u postgres psql`, local peer auth), applied
   `scratch_supabase_stub.sql`, then replayed all 119 pre-`0120` migration files (`0001`-`0119`) in
   filename order verbatim - clean, no manual fixture, no error. Ran the exact verification query
   the commit's own migration header specifies
   (`has_function_privilege('anon', p.oid, 'EXECUTE')` over non-trigger `security definer` functions
   in `public`): **52**, matching the claim exactly, not approximately.

3. **The migration's own revoke list** - counted `47` `revoke` statements in
   `0120_security_definer_functions_anon_grant_table_cleanup.sql` by grep, independent of the
   commit message's prose. `52 (pre-fix anon-executable) - 5 (named exclusions:
   apply_payfast_itn/invite_preview/signups_enabled/start_payfast_checkout/
   unsubscribe_lifecycle_email) = 47` - matches exactly.

4. **Applied the real migration file** (not a hand-copied fragment) to the same scratch database -
   re-ran the identical query: **5**, exactly the 5 named exclusions, confirmed by listing them.

5. **Functional, not just grant-table, verification.** `set role anon; select
   is_platform_admin();` / `select * from platform_admin_companies();` / `select
   is_company_member(<uuid>);` - all three now raise `permission denied for function ...` post-fix
   (pre-fix, re-confirmed these executed with no error, returning `f`/0 rows - the grant really was
   live). `set role authenticated` on the same three calls - unaffected: still returns the correct
   business-logic result (`f` for a non-admin, 0 rows for a non-member), not a new grant-level
   denial. Zero regression for the one role that actually uses these, confirmed directly, not
   inferred.

6. **The two "never had any revoke/grant at all" functions** (`is_company_member`, 0001;
   `tt_is_company_admin`, 0050) - grepped every migration file for any prior `grant`/`revoke`
   statement naming either function: zero hits before `0120`. Claim confirmed, not assumed from the
   commit's own prose.

7. **The "zero RLS policies target anon/public" claim** underpinning the "not independently
   exploitable" severity judgment - independently re-derived, not re-read: extracted every real
   `create policy ... to <role>` clause across all migrations (158 total) - every single one targets
   `authenticated`; none target `anon` or `public`. Confirms a real `anon` RPC call under the old,
   buggy grant table could not have reached a table row an RLS policy would otherwise have blocked
   anyway (though several of the 44 fixed functions also have their own internal `auth.uid()`/
   `is_company_member()`/`is_platform_admin()` gate independent of RLS, as the commit says).

8. **One minor imprecision found in the commit's own prose, not in its fix.** The commit's
   migration header lumps `tt_pack_company`/`tt_person_in_company`/`tt_tender_visible_to` together
   as "harmless id-existence booleans". Checked each definition individually:
   `tt_person_in_company`/`tt_tender_visible_to` do return `boolean` as described, but
   `tt_pack_company(p_pack uuid)` actually `returns uuid` (the pack's owning `company_id`), not a
   boolean - a real id-to-id lookup, not an existence check. Traced its only 5 real call sites
   (`0043`/`0065`/`0066`/`0097`, all inside `before insert` trigger bodies for cross-tenant-integrity
   checks) - never exposed as a policy predicate or a client-callable existence check, so the
   practical severity conclusion (harmless, since `tender_pack` ids are themselves unguessable UUIDs
   and the only thing learned is which company owns a given pack id, with no further anon-reachable
   lookup on that company id since no policy targets `anon`) still holds. The migration's actual fix
   list is unaffected - `tt_pack_company` is still correctly revoked from `anon` in `0120` - this is
   purely a two-word looseness in the explanatory comment ("boolean" vs. "uuid lookup"), not a defect
   in the fix itself. Noted here so it isn't silently carried forward as settled prose if anyone
   re-cites it.

9. **Test suite, re-run for real on current `HEAD` (`389d6a7`), not re-read from the commit's own
   numbers** (which were correct for the commit's own point in history - `389/389`/`50 files` - but
   stale now that later passes in this chain added more tests): `npx tsc --noEmit` - 0 errors.
   `npx eslint .` - 0 errors, the same 3 pre-existing warnings. `npx vitest run` - **474/474, 60
